articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO's exit rattles AI stocks
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO's exit rattles AI stocks
articles.content_orig:
Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience.
His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Jensen Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Jensen Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Jensen Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution.
Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Jensen Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.
"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Jensen Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games.
Jensen Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.
In the process, Jensen Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps.
To expand his customer base, Jensen Huang designated compute capacity to a number of so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , putting equity into the companies and helping them build big businesses around renting out GPUs.
Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google.
Jensen Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private.
In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world.
"He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market."
When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Jensen Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Jensen Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.
One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Jensen Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated.
Jensen Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Jensen Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.
Alice Huang, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Jensen Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.
U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Jensen Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday.
"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Jensen Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Jensen Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son.
On the deal-making side, Jensen Huang's top lieutenants were finance chief Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Jensen Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Jensen Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief
articles.content_orig:
Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation here.
Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% on Thursday, sending the company's value below $4 trillion in market cap after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair . The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed , according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China.
The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times.
Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.
Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia's stock by half from $400 to $200.
Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday that Huang's alleged affair with a direct report means it is "much tougher for the board to leave him in position."
Huang was central to Nvidia's rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.
Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the "visionary" to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO.
"Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they're in the position that they're in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago," Rasgon said. "Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don't intuitively know who that person would be."
Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang's resignation , adding further pressure to the CEO and the company.
Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia's lack of a succession plan makes the stock "uninvestable."
"Nvidia doesn't have that person in place, and so it's going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations," Reyle told CNBC's "Access Middle East."
"Or they're going to have to move on from him, and that's just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn't make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable."
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: AI’s Central Bank Is in Crisis. Intel and These Stocks Are Feeling the Pain.
articles.title_zh: AI’s Central Bank Is in Crisis. Intel and These Stocks Are Feeling the Pain.
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom?
Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system.
Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.
A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion.
But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said.
"Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said.
Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against.
And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts.
In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy.
"I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit.
Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years. Hedge funds and retail investors are making risky bets even riskier by taking on debt to buy stocks or investing in funds that have embedded leverage.
Nvidia is at the center of all of that. The company has repeatedly stepped in to help backstop smaller AI companies known as neoclouds, which build data centers using Nvidia chips and lease capacity to other firms. Among other obligations, Nvidia disclosed in July that it has committed to buy up to $36 billion in cloud services from those companies. That helps Nvidia ensure that there will be more customers for its AI chips, and it helps those companies find easier financing.
Wu and others refer to these kinds of arrangements as circular financing. When business is growing, it can be productive for bigger firms to help their customers buy their products. But if Nvidia couldn't honor its obligations, it would ripple through the firms that borrowed the money and the banks that lent to it. Relatively opaque private credit funds have also lent heavily into the AI boom, and how they would fare is a subject of debate among regulators.
Nvidia didn't reveal its specific partners, but some neoclouds such as CoreWeave and IREN have separately disclosed their relationships with the bigger firm.
Many neoclouds have been under stress in recent weeks. The cost of insuring CoreWeave debt , as measured by credit-default spreads, rose by 94% — nearly doubling — from Oct. 1 to Nov. 5, before settling, according to LSEG data. The price of an IREN convertible bond maturing in 2029 fell 23% from Nov. 3 to Nov. 5, amid a 26% decline in the company's share price.
Nvidia's other obligations include a $105 billion phased guarantee to a major data center project in Ohio planned by OpenAI and SB Energy, subject to certain conditions. Nvidia promised to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program by Wall Street financial firms.
These obligations come in different forms and are unlikely to come due all at once, if ever. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School finance professor, estimates them at $400 billion overall.
That is a huge sum, but still a small fraction of the roughly $3.9 trillion market capitalization Nvidia has even after its stock decline. "The company would have to get to the brink of extinction before all these guarantees come into jeopardy."
"I don't want to say it's a safe system, but I do want to say there's a lot of equity in the system right now," Van Nieuwerburgh said.
But in the past few days, Nvidia's troubles have separated it from the pack. Most neoclouds' equity prices have recovered this week as Nvidia's share price has fallen. That suggests investors see Nvidia's problems as specific to the company, for now.
Meanwhile the basic laws of economics are driving other firms to try to move into Nvidia's lucrative chips business. AMD , Broadcom , Intel , Google , Microsoft , and OpenAI all have efforts underway to build their own AI chips, Van Nieuwerburgh said.
Over time, they could replace Nvidia's products. That could cap the economic fallout of any potential troubles at the company.
And yet it's impossible to entirely write off the financial risks of the AI trade suddenly hitting a wall, added Van Nieuwerburgh, who spoke to me over Zoom from the sidelines of a bimonthly meeting of finance officials in Basel, Switzerland.
Central bankers "are clearly very, very, very anxious about this and thinking hard about these questions," he said.

articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Stock Dives. Nvidia's Huang Issue Spells Trouble for Other AI Plays.
articles.content_orig:
Investing.com -- CoreWeave shares fell 15% on Thursday, giving back much of the previous session's nearly 25% rally, as Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO rattled the AI infrastructure sector and disappointing guidance from Nebius added to investor concerns.

Nvidia confirmed that Huang is stepping down, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. The departure marks a major leadership change at the world's dominant AI chipmaker and introduces fresh uncertainty for companies whose businesses are closely tied to Nvidia's ecosystem.
CoreWeave is particularly exposed to developments at Nvidia, which is both a strategic investor and a key technology partner. The chipmaker also plays a broader role in financing and supporting the AI infrastructure ecosystem, making the leadership upheaval potentially significant beyond Nvidia itself.
The concerns extend to the financial relationships underpinning the AI infrastructure boom, with investors already scrutinizing the extent to which Nvidia-backed financing helps sustain demand for its own chips and the infrastructure built around them.
The pressure was compounded by Nebius Group's quarterly results and outlook. Although the Amsterdam-based AI cloud provider reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, above analyst expectations of $907.5 million, its updated spending plans and delays in bringing additional capacity online disappointed investors.
Nebius said some third-party capacity originally expected to become available this year has been pushed into the first half of 2027. The company expects to reach its target of more than $7 billion in annualized run-rate revenue approximately two months later than initially planned.

At the same time, Nebius raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to approximately $27 billion, up from a previous range of $20 billion to $25 billion, and projected spending of $40 billion to $45 billion next year.
The company expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, while saying that customer prepayments and asset-backed financing will cover approximately 75% to 85% of next year's spending.
The outlook highlights the enormous capital requirements and execution challenges facing AI cloud providers, even as demand for computing capacity remains strong.
CoreWeave had offered investors a dose of reassurance just one session earlier. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168% year over year, and raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13 billion to $13.3 billion. Its revenue backlog reached approximately $132.5 billion.
CEO Michael Intrator also said the company was largely sold out through 2027, reinforcing the argument that demand for AI computing continues to outstrip available supply.
Thursday's reversal suggests that strong demand and growing backlogs are not enough to shield the sector from broader concerns about its dependence on Nvidia, financing requirements and the pace at which new infrastructure can be delivered.

articles.title_orig: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:

After being moored along Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary this week, the 120-metre-long (400-foot-long) cargo ship Karin set sail for Russia.
The vessel was laden with a bulk cargo of white powder that can be forged into weapons which are vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine .
Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminium, goes into products from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones.
A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland operates as Europe’s biggest alumina refinery, regularly sending shiploads of the substance directly to St Petersburg and other Russian ports.
Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy . That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where experts say some ends up in weapons.
“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies," said Irish politician Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party.
“It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”
Ireland faces mounting calls to halt the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.
Irish government minister Niall Collins said that "there’s absolutely no evidence" the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to publish the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.
Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”
Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.
The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the US and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic.
The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.
These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories – one in Australia, the other in Ukraine – stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40 per cent, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17 per cent of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.
An investigation by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times , published earlier this year, found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.
“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.
Standing next to Irish President Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Mr Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”
Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it is not, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government has not published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex”.
“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said in October in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.
The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.
A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material”.
Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Mr Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse”.
Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Ms Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalisation of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should”, if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine”.

articles.title_orig: Google Agrees to Privacy in Spirit Airlines Data Sale
articles.title_zh: Google Agrees to Privacy in Spirit Airlines Data Sale
articles.content_orig:
The revised agreement resolves union objections over AI training use of employee files and still needs bankruptcy court approval
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Google $GOOGL , a unit of Alphabet , agreed to add privacy protections for former Spirit Airlines employees to its $10 million purchase of the bankrupt carrier's data, according to The Wall Street Journal .
Spirit filed the revised agreement Monday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in New York, according to The Wall Street Journal. It settles complaints raised by the unions for Spirit's pilots and flight attendants, which had cautioned that workers' personal records would be used to train commercial AI tools. The deal still requires bankruptcy court approval.
Under the new terms, the sale leaves out a range of worker records, including medical files, drug and alcohol test results, investigations tied to labor matters, records of grievances and arbitration, performance reviews and payroll, among other employment-related materials, according to The Wall Street Journal. An independent verifier will examine how the data is put to use and confirm that confidentiality and security obligations are being met.
A Spirit spokesperson said the carrier welcomed settling the unions' disputes about the "sale of deidentified data" while it works to get the most value it can for creditors, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The unions argued that the original terms gave consumers stronger privacy safeguards than they gave airline employees, according to The Wall Street Journal. Over 120 congressional lawmakers wrote to Spirit and Google in October, pressing for stronger safeguards for ex-employees.
"Worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a whole new worker's rights issue," Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, said Tuesday, according to The Wall Street Journal. "Without our union, there would have been no one to speak for workers in this fire sale of their private information. We fought and we won brand new protections."
Google won the August bankruptcy auction for Spirit's digital archives, according to The Wall Street Journal. The archives contain decades of payroll, travel and recruiting files, along with about 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts and millions of other digital items. Google has said the purchase excludes personal information, and that it intends to apply the data toward improving its products and AI models.
Google agreed to pay $10 million for Spirit's internal business data after winning the auction. AI hiring platform Mercor was the runner-up with a $7.5 million offer. Google said a third party would scrub personally identifiable information from the data before handoff.
Spirit ceased operations earlier this year after a government rescue package collapsed, leaving roughly 17,000 employees and contractors without work.

articles.title_orig: Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company
articles.title_zh: Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company
articles.content_orig:
Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang .
Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.
The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.
In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had been uncooperative. Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.
Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.
Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”
She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.
Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

articles.title_orig: Toyota to bring 'really cute' tiny trucks favored by Trump to the US
articles.title_zh: Toyota to bring 'really cute' tiny trucks favored by Trump to the US
articles.content_orig:
Imagine a pickup truck, but much smaller, lighter and lacking any frills. It’s a vehicle that people in Japan have been using for decades. And now Toyota wants to sell one in the United States.
This week, the automaker introduced a tiny pickup truck inspired by Japanese “Kei” trucks, under the Scion brand that Toyota shuttered in 2016. The vehicle, the Scion KEI-01, will go on sale next year.
Kei vehicles (pronounced like the letter “K”) are a distinct category of small cars, vans and trucks in Japan and other Asian countries. These vehicles have long had a cult following in the United States. Even President Trump showed adoration , calling them “really cute” and “sort of like the Beetle used to be.” He made the remarks last year after a visit to Japan and mused about finding a way to have them sold in the United States.
But buying and using one of these vehicles in the United States is not easy. Car buffs who want Kei cars and trucks typically import vehicles that are at least 25 years old from Japan to take advantage of a provision in U.S. law that exempts older vehicles from federal safety and emissions standards.
Toyota says the KEI-01 will be assembled in Indiana and will qualify as a “low speed vehicle” under federal regulations. Vehicles in that category must have a top speed of 25 miles an hour and are generally forbidden from roads with speed limits of more than 35 m.p.h. Such vehicles also do not have to meet the same safety and other standards as regular cars.
The KEI-01 is in many ways the opposite of traditional U.S. pickup trucks like the Ford F-150 or Chevrolet Silverado, which over the past several decades have become bigger, heavier and more expensive. Most automakers have found that it is much easier to make a profit on larger vehicles because they tend not to cost much more to make than smaller ones but can be sold for a lot more money.

articles.title_orig: I tried Google’s AI glasses and Meta’s finally got real competition
articles.title_zh: I tried Google’s AI glasses and Meta’s finally got real competition
articles.content_orig:
The AI experience is better, the privacy protections are more proactive, and they’re still stylish.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
It’s a weird time to launch a new pair of smart glasses.
These last few years, Meta has been the dominant player in pushing a fragile smart glasses resurgence. Unfortunately, its privacy reputation led to the “pervert glasses” moniker. Smart glasses have never been more unpopular.
But in the past week, I’ve been demoing some new smart glasses from Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster. Some are retro chic frames. Others have the same Y2K vibe as the Matrix films. All were made by Samsung and have Google’s Gemini built in via Android XR, Google’s platform for smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets.
The AI demos are better than I expected. In one, I’m sitting in an avant-garde art installation as creepy heads float above my head. On the loudspeaker, words blare in French, Spanish, Korean, and German. Pressing two fingers to my temple, Gemini starts translating each language seamlessly in real time. In another demo, a TV chef cooks a “monster pasta” recipe in Korean while people have a conversation behind me. Music in another language is playing overhead. This exact scenario tripped up the Meta Ray-Ban Display’s translation capabilities when I was on vacation. Here it’s no big deal. I don’t even have to specify the languages I need translated or, as with Meta’s glasses, download a specific language pair to translate. I sit at another table with an English speaker, a Thai speaker, and the glasses translate everything they say to me — correctly — into Japanese.
But I was most surprised that the glasses automatically redact faces from any photo or video to protect bystander privacy. I asked Gemini to identify my video director, Owen Grove. Gemini told me it knew I was looking at a person, but it can’t identify him because of privacy protections. We pull up a picture of our editor-in-chief, Nilay Patel. There, too, Gemini said that for privacy reasons, it can’t identify a person from a photo either.
Meta’s glasses also can’t do this. But what’s striking here is that Google is making an active choice to take facial recognition completely off the table.
The Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses have the customary privacy LED light that lights up whenever there’s an intent to save visual data. Like Meta’s glasses, there’ll be protections in place to disable the glasses if tampering is detected. However, when I sit down to chat with Juston Payne, Google’s senior director of product management for XR, he says Google intends to go much further than the LED light.
“Somebody might come up with some solution [to tamper with privacy LEDs] that our algorithms can’t detect, so then the question becomes: So what can we do?” says Payne.
“We’re not going to target ads on it. We’re not going to train Gemini on it. Humans aren’t going to be able to use it to improve the models. We’re also redacting faces before they actually go to the server in the first place, which then gets ahead of certain things that can obviously go sideways if you don’t take those steps proactively.”
It’s not just faces that’ll get redacted either. Payne tells me that ambient noise — like bystander conversations — will also get scrubbed. The glasses will only process audio from the glasses-wearer using beam-forming mics. Camera and mic access will also require opt-in permissions.
Alone, these are a bold departure from Meta’s approach to smart glasses. Locally redacting faces and ambient audio, for example, is a conscious choice to give up a valuable source of training data. Google could leave it at that, and Android XR would already have a leg up in the privacy discussion. But Payne says Google plans on using its entire platform to disincentivize glassholes.
For example, YouTube will crack down on any creepy videos featuring harassment or unwanted sexualization, regardless of how they’re captured. Google Shopping and Google Ads won’t allow sales or ads for accessories like lens covers for privacy LED lights. Google Play policies will prohibit third-party apps from enabling social livestreaming, real-time facial identification, or changing anything about how the LED light functions. Payne also says third-party apps requiring camera or mic API access will need further review to prove they’re being used responsibly. This is less of a concern right now, but it’s a future-focused stance for other Android XR devices or even with devices like Xreal’s Aura glasses.
It’s hard to gauge how effective this privacy policy will be with the public. We’ll have to see how it’s received. It’s much more expansive than Meta’s more reactive approach so far. Granted, Meta doesn’t have its own app store or a computing platform quite like Android. This still underscores how much more Meta could’ve been doing all along.
The one area Meta truly nailed with smart glasses has been style. The company, through its partnership with EssilorLuxottica, has over 100 combinations of frames and lenses. Samsung’s partnerships with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster aren’t too shabby to look at. Warby Parker has three designs and three colors: green, brown, and black. Gentle Monster has six frames — including two that are very Y2K — with bolder designs, colors, and tinted lens options. The Warby Parker collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster starts at $449.
Style-wise, I found both collections were fetching. Warby Parker was a bit more everyday, whereas Gentle Monster felt a bit more editorial and runway-ready. Most people should be able to find a look that fits their needs.
The glasses are fairly lightweight (for smart glasses) at 41g. Battery life is estimated at around nine hours, while the cases support up to seven extra charges. Sound quality is pretty good, and the 12MP ultrawide camera takes decent photos and video with image stabilization. So, head tilters rejoice! Your accidental Dutch-angle photos will be straightened.
Where Android XR excels is that Gemini on the glasses is, so far, more capable than Meta AI on the Ray-Bans. I was able to look at an event flyer for a concert in Mumbai, have Gemini add the details to Google Calendar, and then look up flight details to India. It gave me turn-by-turn walking directions while also telling me the event schedule for the Whitney Museum. Beginning a live translation doesn’t require me to download a specific language pair onto my phone like with the Ray-Bans. I was also surprised to see Gemini occasionally correct itself in real-time when it made a mistake, or ask me to get a different view of an object I was trying to identify so it could deliver a more accurate answer.
Low-vision and blind users aren’t left out either. The glasses feature Google’s Guided Vision, which offers conversational audio descriptions of environments and surroundings. Android XR is also collaborating with Aira, which allows users to stream what they’re seeing using the camera to a real-time human interpreter. At launch, this particular feature will be for Android users only, but otherwise the glasses will work regardless of your phone.
Leaving my hands-on, it’s never been clearer that technology isn’t currently the issue with smart glasses. Whether or not this form factor takes off will boil down to culture, privacy, and usefulness. And on that front, this space has been stagnating a bit because Meta has been the sole big player setting the tone and pushing the conversation. The Android XR approach is notably different, and serious competition for Meta is excellent for consumers. All that’s left is to see whose approach wins.
You can preorder Gentle Monster and Warby Parker smart glasses starting today, and the devices are expected to ship starting December 10th.

articles.title_orig: Apple HomeView Review: A Versatile Smart Display And Siri-Powered Home Hub
articles.title_zh: Apple HomeView Review: A Versatile Smart Display And Siri-Powered Home Hub
articles.content_orig:
The company’s smart screen debut heavily relies on an iPhone or iPad — for better and for worse.
Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years. By the time its debut home hub device arrives this week, the company will be nearly a decade behind its main rivals in the space. In true Apple fashion, it refused to rush new products just because most of the competition was doing it. Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities .
Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device. That means you'll need either an iPhone or an iPad to mirror apps using technology similar to CarPlay. As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others. You'll also need to have some smart home devices to make the most of the smart display and be willing to use Safari as your recipe box. If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family.
I have fond memories of the iMac G4 . It was the first computer I used in a design lab in college, and I loved how I could reposition the display to suit the task at hand. The first time I saw the HomeView, those memories flooded back. Apple's smart home display doesn't exactly replicate the G4 styling, but it's close enough for a decent nostalgia hit for me.
The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display. At least, that's if you get the tabletop version. The wall-mounted option is just the screen, and you'll have to pay at least $59.95 for a mount. Every version of the HomeView has two full-range drivers in the display itself. The base houses additional components, like a down-firing woofer and a pair of force-canceling passive radiators for fuller sound with more bass than the wall-mounted models.
That display has an LED-backlit multi-touch IPS panel that offers a 1,088 x 1,088 resolution at 200 pixels per inch. Apple says it also added an oleophobic fingerprint-resistant coating to cut down on grime from everyday use. There's an ambient light sensor that enables the HomeView to adjust both brightness and warmth as needed. If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display. The company believes this makes it perfect for a nightstand, if you're willing to have a camera pointed at or near your bed.
The HomeView's display has bezels like an iPad and the shape of a large Apple Watch. Unlike either of those devices, though, it has no physical buttons for controls. All of the interaction is done via swipes and taps on the touchscreen itself, or, as I'll elaborate on in a bit, with your voice. And unlike that iMac I'm nostalgic for, you can only tilt the display — you can't adjust its height. While that will suit most of your needs, I'm sure there are a lot of people who would've liked the ability to change the height or rotate the screen as well. Once you do adjust the way it tilts, a built-in accelerometer detects the new angle and alters the audio performance of the display's two drivers to match it.
Another item to discuss in terms of design is the HomeView's lone port. Around back, there's a single USB-C jack for power. Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter. If you opt for the USB-C wall mount, which already costs $59.99, you'll need to purchase the power adapter separately. The company offers a 40W dynamic power adapter (up to 60W max) for $39 while the minimum required power supply ( 20W ) will cost you $19. Obviously, the AC wired and PoE (power over Ethernet) wired mounts won't need a power adapter.
And lastly, there's the matter of color. For the standard (table or countertop) version of HomeView, you can choose from Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink or Space Gray options. On those, the sides and back of the display match the base. For the wall-mounted version, you can only pick between Silver and Space Gray. And, just in case you need the reminder, both HomeView models are the same price ($299).
One of the HomeView's most helpful traits is its ability to put Siri AI front and center in your home. The smart device runs on Apple's A18 chip, the processor that debuted with the iPhone 16 line in 2024. The company is using it here for its Secure Exclaves which give it the ability to process camera and microphone feeds on-device in a manner that can't be accessed by Apple. The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system.
That's important, because Siri AI now has access to more of your personal data, like your conversations in Messages, info from your Calendar invites and other bits of "personal context" from various apps. Of course, you have to opt-in to all of this by enabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone or iPad, and you can limit which apps Siri can index data from. If you do decide to use the system, I can attest that it works well on the HomeView, though it's merely another vessel for the larger AI system.
During a lengthy conversation about lighthouses in North Carolina, Siri gave me information about visiting a variety of locations in the state. It provided information that I didn't specifically ask for, like which ones were still active, and got more comprehensive when my follow-up query was a bit vague. For example, when I asked "Which lighthouse is the easiest to get to?" Siri responded with both a list of ones you can park close to and highlighted the one that requires the least amount of climbing.
Siri was able to check my calendar to see if I was free to take the trip on a certain date and provided travel time from my house (including follow-up questions about the cities I'd pass through). I was finally able to stump the AI when I asked about "good hotels" near the Currituck Beach Lighthouse in Corolla, but even still, things felt more natural and conversational than interactions I've had with Siri in the past.
At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info. When I asked about driving time or my schedule, a preview of the best route and the specific day on my calendar popped up respectively. What's more, I got a notification on my phone from the Home app letting me know Siri responded to a request for personal content. But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities. These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools.
One final note on security: Since the HomeView is heavily reliant on an iPhone or iPad, those devices must be nearby and recently unlocked (and enrolled in the shared home) for Siri to access personal data. The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to know who's speaking, and to know when they walk away, so prying eyes can't see your texts if they rush over after you've been looking at Messages or other potentially sensitive apps. Guests or family members who don't have an iPhone or iPad can still use basic functions (control smart home devices, check weather, play music, etc), including asking Siri rudimentary questions.
When I first spent time with the HomeView last month, the feature I was most excited about was the recipe integration in Safari. I'm happy to report that feeling remains, for the most part, but there's one caveat that does impact the overall experience.

articles.title_orig: Mammoth crowds greet Pope Leo on return to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Mammoth crowds greet Pope Leo on return to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Just a year and a half into his papacy and less than a month after surgeons removed a lobe of his right lung , Pope Leo XIV, the first pontiff born in the United States, touched down in his homeland on Wednesday.
Yet instead of setting foot on American soil, he arrived in Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a citizen in 2015.
“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, speaking on Wednesday evening to Peru’s president, civic leaders and diplomats at the Gran Teatro Nacional, a theater and concert hall in the country’s capital, Lima. One of his biggest applause lines was when he referred to Peru as “my homeland.”
Having turned out record crowds at Masses in Argentina, the pope flew from Buenos Aires to Lima on Wednesday afternoon, reaching the final country of his 12-day tour of South America. The pope emerged at the top of the stairs next to a sign on the side of his plane that read “Pontifex Maximus,” and was greeted by Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and a chorus of singing children on a red carpet at the Callao Air Base near Lima.
As his motorcade made its way through city streets under gray skies, about 3 million people lined the roads, according to local authorities, holding up cellphones as they waited for a glimpse of the pontiff.
His choice to visit Peru so soon after becoming pope — while deferring a visit to the country of his birth — underscored the deep emotional ties he feels to the place that formed him as a priest.

articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) - Gold prices are trading at session lows on Thursday morning following the release of worse than expected labor market data after the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits came in above economists’ forecasts.
Initial claims for state unemployment benefits came in at seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ending November 7, the Labor Department announced on Thursday. The number was above expectations, as consensus estimates forecasted a reading of 195,000 claims. The previous week’s figure was revised to 191,000.
Spot gold was setting fresh session lows following the 8:30 am ET data release, and last traded at $3,903.98 per ounce for a loss of 2.11% on the daily chart.
Meanwhile, the four-week moving average for new claims – often viewed as a more reliable measure of the labor market since it flattens week-to-week volatility – came in at 195,250, against expectations for 192,500 and following the previous week’s revised 195,250 level.
Continuing jobless claims, which represent the number of people already receiving benefits, were at 1.697 million during the week ending October 31 against expectations for 1.710, and following the previous week’s revised 1.717 million level.

articles.title_orig: US envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: US envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
Two days of talks in Abu Dhabi did not appear to produce a breakthrough.
LONDON -- President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on Thursday morning ahead of a planned meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, following two days of trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi that seemingly produced no major diplomatic breakthrough .
Trump's envoys are expected to travel to Dublin, Ireland, later on Thursday, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Witkoff and Kushner were greeted in Moscow by Kirill Dmitriev, the CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, who has been involved in revived U.S.-Russian bilateral relations since Trump's return to office in January 2025.
This week's meetings in Abu Dhabi were the first trilateral talks held since February. The parties agreed a new prisoner exchange deal -- the largest of the war to date, according to Kushner -- and discussed issues including security guarantees for Ukraine and broader European security arrangements, according to readouts from the delegations.
Kushner said in a post to X on Wednesday that the prisoner exchange "will reunite families, build trust, and create momentum toward peace."
"Bringing Ukraine and Russia back together for the first trilateral talks since February was an important step. The discussions were serious, detailed, and frank. Both countries shared specific ideas to narrow the gaps and find a path to end the war," he added.
"In close coordination with Ukraine and our European partners, we have aligned on proposals we will discuss with President Putin in Moscow tomorrow, followed by consultations with President Zelenskyy," Kushner wrote, though acknowledged that "significant differences remain" between the combatants.
As Russia's full-scale invasion nears a potential fifth anniversary, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on key negotiating issues. Those include the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory in the east and southeast of the country, security guarantees from foreign partners to prevent renewed Russian aggression, Ukraine's ambition to join NATO and the size and capabilities of Kyiv's armed forces.
Zelenskyy arrived in Dublin on Wednesday, following a visit to Denmark. The Ukrainian president is expected to meet with European leaders gathered there for the European Political Community event, which will see around 40 heads of state and government travel to Dublin.
In a post to social media on Wednesday, Zelenskyy said it was "essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war -- that is Russia -- so that Russia ends the war of its own making."
The Ukrainian leader said in a post to X that he expected to meet with Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday. "We are working to bring peace closer. Thank you to everyone who helps and supports Ukraine," he wrote.
Both sides continued their long-range strike campaigns overnight.
Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 123 drones, of which 73 were jet powered, alongside a mix of Iskander ballistic missiles, Banderol cruise missiles and Zirkon anti-ship missiles.
Defenders intercepted or suppressed 89 drones, of which 51 were jet powered, and five Banderol missiles, the air force said. It reported impacts in 17 locations.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a post to Telegram that one person was killed and seven others were injured in the capital's western Solomianskyi district when a drone strike set fire to an apartment block.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and other targets in the Rivne region, and said that one person was injured by Russian strikes in the Zhytomyr region.
Zelenskyy said in a post to Telegram that Ukrainian forces had recorded "significant disruptions" and 100 mile per hour speed restrictions in the operation of the military-grade Starshield satellite network -- which is run through Elon Musk's company SpaceX -- "for several days" along the entire frontline and in Russian-occupied Ukraine.
"This primarily means a significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones," Zelenskyy said. "Unfortunately, there have already been strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time.
"This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine. We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side," Zelenskyy added.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said its forces downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. The craft were shot down over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Tula, Oryol, Rostov and Moscow regions, plus occupied Crimea, it said.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in posts to Telegram that at least five Ukrainian drones were shot down over the capital overnight.
Russia's federal air transport agency, Rosaviatsiya, said temporary flight restrictions were introduced at two of Moscow's four international airports; Zhukovsky and Domodedovo. Flight restrictions were not put in place at Vnukovo airport, where Witkoff and Kushner landed.
Restrictions were also put in place for airports in Penza, Saransk, Saratov and Kaluga, Rosaviatsiya said.
One person was injured during a drone attack in the border region of Belgorod and another person was injured by a strike in the neighboring Kursk region, local officials said.

articles.title_orig: Two men guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target journalists and lawyer
articles.title_zh: Two men guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target journalists and lawyer
articles.content_orig:
Two Iranian men have been convicted of spying for an Iranian intelligence service by carrying out surveillance on journalists and a lawyer in the UK.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted of "assisting a foreign intelligence service" at Woolwich Crown Court on Thursday.
They were tasked by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) with monitoring the targets. Sepahvand intended to carry out a "violent attack" against at least one of them, while Manesh helped with planning.
A third man, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was cleared of the same charge.
Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.
Police seized 534GB of data that showed Sapahvand and Manesh were given documents that included pictures of targets, their work addresses, the make and colour of their cars and the names of pets. They then used ChatGPT to carry out further research.
The pair, from west London, are asylum seekers who had been granted temporary leave to remain. Sepahvand arrived in the UK in a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.
Sepahvand conducted surveillance and reconnaissance in preparation for inflicting violence on several "subjects" in the UK.
These included journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, who worked for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran international, Jonathan Turner, a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, as well as a media production professional.
Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, the senior national co-ordinator for Counter-Terrorism Policing, said it was the first time ChatGPT case search history had been presented in a state threat case.
She added: "It's something we're beginning to see more of as AI tools become more widely available and people become more aware of them."
It was clear from the evidence at the trial that at times Sepahvand felt he was being mistreated by his Iranian handlers, who had not paid him.
Evans said: "This is a trend we see in these types of cases where people get involved in work on behalf of foreign states and they're often promised money and lots of other things but they rarely receive what they've been offered."
Sepahvand had claimed he participated in the spying out of fear of the consequences of refusing but the prosecution described this as "entirely bogus".
In voice notes sent to an Iranian contact, he said he had been promised that a conviction for theft in Iran would be "sorted out" - which prosecutors said was part of his motivation for conducting the surveillance.
Sepahvand also asked for £150,000 in exchange for "finishing off" a target, stressing that he would "do it".
Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service's counter-terrorism division, said the two men had been promised rewards for sending intelligence back to contacts in Iran.
"Sepahvand himself was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit serious violence against their targets," he said.
"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place.
"Cases like this show Iranian intelligence's willingness to use proxies to target the regime's critics abroad."
Sepahvand and Manesh will be sentenced at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Stock tanks after new affair allegations, board reportedly preparing to oust Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust chief executive officer Jensen Huang following disclosures regarding two extramarital relationships, including one with a senior corporate subordinate and another involving a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy , as reported by The Wall Street Journal .
The board's impending move follows reporting from The New York Times detailing that Huang maintained an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. The relationship has been discussed inside the company, according to five people who worked at the chip-maker.
Powell, 48, reports directly to the 63-year-old CEO. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people.
According to sources familiar with the matter, Huang and Powell were observed behaving affectionately at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March.
A bystander recorded the interaction on a smartphone, after which members of Huang's personal security detail sequestered the individual and offered them a non-disclosure agreement to sign, according to three people briefed on the incident. The New York Times noted it had not viewed the video.
During that same conference in March, Powell — who joined Nvidia in 2008 and was promoted to lead its healthcare unit in 2017 — delivered a presentation on artificial intelligence applications in biology that featured cartoon depictions of Huang.
Such relationships conflict directly with Nvidia's corporate code of conduct, which explicitly directs employees to avoid situations, including personal relationships, that generate internal conflicts. The policy states that the company "promptly investigates reports of misconduct."
When reached by phone on Wednesday by The New York Times to address his relationship with Powell, Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," before hanging up.
This development compounds an existing crisis surrounding the chip-making giant . Earlier this week, Huang admitted in a memo to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife , following revelations regarding his relationship with Alice Huang — no relation — who U.S. intelligence has said facilitated shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms as part of a foreign intelligence operation. China has denied the espionage claims.
Nvidia's board previously launched an internal investigation into the matter led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. Additionally, Republican leaders of three House committees have called for Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing regarding his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset.
The revelations have drawn criticism from lawmakers, investors and Nvidia's board over Huang's conduct.
Nvidia shares fell approximately 8 percent in after-hours trading following Wednesday's reports. The stock has wiped out more than $300 billion in market value since disclosures regarding Alice Huang first emerged.
If Huang leaves, it would create an immediate leadership gap at the $4 trillion chipmaker, which is the driving force behind the global AI boom and the technological rivalry between the U.S. and China.

articles.title_orig: Italy seeks to curb impact of hoax bomb alerts as more threats received
articles.title_zh: Italy seeks to curb impact of hoax bomb alerts as more threats received
articles.content_orig:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.
The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools   - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spoken of "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern".
Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government.
La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake".
According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued.

articles.title_orig: 30% of iPhone Duo buyers may have returned it, but I don’t think Apple should worry
articles.title_zh: 30% of iPhone Duo buyers may have returned it, but I don’t think Apple should worry
articles.content_orig:
A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund.
While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying …
Following a report by The Verge on iPhone Duo buyers who opted to return the device for a refund within Apple’s 14-day “no questions asked” period, we thought it would be interesting to get a sense of how many people may have done this.
9to5Mac readers were always likely to have had their fingers hovering over the pre-order button for the best shot at taking early delivery, with the first of these having hit the end of the 14-day window. We ask those of you who fall into this category to tell us whether you kept or returned the device.
With close to 6,000 total votes, the results showed that close to a third of you returned your Duo.
For any other device, that would be a disastrous return rate. For the Duo, however, I don’t think it’s terribly surprising.
As we noted yesterday, Apple described the iPhone Duo as “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.” The size of that change shows up in a whole range of ways, from the weight of the device through the changed aspect ratio of the front display to a completely new way of using an iPhone.
Throw in the extremely high price tag, and I’ve always suspected that a significant number of iPhone Duo buyers would be viewing it as an experiment rather than a committed purchase. Our own Ryan Christoffel is an example of that “try it and see” attitude. One week in, he’s reached an interim conclusion that it’s probably not for him .
For those who’ve decided to return it, a number of readers shared their reasons.
“Returned it – I can’t go back to Touch ID.”
“Returned it. Cameras are key for me.”
“I want to like it, but I just can’t get there. It’s awkward, and the outside screen is way too small.”
“Returned it. Not for me. I do not want to open the phone every time I want a larger screen and Apple made the outer display much less usable than it should be with that silly permanent dock. I also use my phones left-handed.”
“During a vacation in Morocco, we spent a night camping in the Sahara Desert. I was extremely careful with the phone and tried to avoid using it in the sand altogether. However, on the second day, when I opened it inside the tent, I heard a crunching sound coming from the hinge. Sand had somehow gotten inside. I tried everything I could to clean it, but nothing worked. The inner display was still functioning perfectly, but the phone would no longer open all the way. Even worse, when I tried to close it, I had to force it shut.”
For me personally, it couldn’t be my only phone, given the priority I place on the device as a camera, but I am still lusting after it. Given the continued extended delivery times – with random checks showing shipping in late January – I don’t think Apple has much to worry about here.

articles.title_orig: Noctua launches $25 NT-CP1 carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM5 and AM4
articles.title_zh: Noctua launches $25 NT-CP1 carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM5 and AM4
articles.content_orig:
Noctua says its NT-CP1 thermal pad improves contact through repeated thermal cycles.
A 90 µm thermal pad designed to replace CPU thermal paste.
Noctua has introduced the NT-CP1 AM5/4 carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD Ryzen processors. Developed with Carbice, the pad measures 33 × 33 mm and is 90 µm thick. Its suggested retail price is $24.95 in the US and €24.95 in Europe.
We covered the Noctua and Carbice partnership in June, when the companies planned a September release. The November announcement now provides pricing and final dimensions. The pad supports both AM5 and AM4 processors.
According to Noctua, the NT-CP1 improves thermal contact over the first few hundred to a few thousand thermal cycles. Its carbon nanotubes gradually conform to microscopic surface irregularities. The company says performance then stays stable for years without replacement.
The pad combines carbon nanotubes with an aluminum support layer and a phase-change polymer coating. Installation follows a peel, press and peel process. The slightly tacky coating helps keep the pad in place while mounting the cooler.
Noctua says the coating makes the contact surfaces electrically non-conductive before use, provided the polymer layer is not penetrated. This qualification is relevant when comparing it with other carbon and graphite pads. The announcement focuses on installation and long-term stability rather than quantified temperature gains over thermal paste.
Carbice manufactures the NT-CP1 in the United States using recycled aluminum and waste carbon gas to grow the nanotubes. Noctua says the pad can enter standard aluminum recycling streams. The AM5/4 version has been tuned and validated for AMD Ryzen CPUs and APUs.
